what: Cirrus Logic designs chips that handle sound and power in portable devices. Its audio chips process and amplify what a phone plays and records, and its power conversion chips manage how efficiently the device uses its battery. It designs the chips and has them manufactured by others.
customers: Smartphone and portable device manufacturers, overwhelmingly Apple, which accounts for the large majority of revenue, along with Android handset makers and laptop manufacturers.
money: Amplifiers, codecs and digital signal processing for playback, recording and noise handling.
Power conversion, camera control and haptic driver chips.
moat: Audio chips are co-designed with the customer’s device over years, tuned to its specific acoustic design, and the software stack around them is custom. That makes a mid-cycle supplier change practically impossible. Cirrus has held its position across many generations of the same customer’s products, which is evidence the relationship is technical rather than merely commercial.
risks: Customer concentration is the dominant risk: the large majority of revenue comes from one customer, who designs its own silicon in other areas and has the capability to do so here.
Revenue has been essentially flat, between $1.8B and $2.0B for five years, tracking its customer’s unit volumes rather than growing.
Only three analysts cover the stock, so the $136.67 average target rests on minimal coverage.
Smartphone unit volumes globally are mature, which caps the addressable market without new content per device.
Chip content decisions are made years ahead, so a lost design win is invisible until the revenue disappears.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 14.5 times earnings, 10.1 times EV/EBITDA and 10.9 times free cash flow — modest for a chip designer with these margins.
A net margin of 20.8% and free cash flow of $526.2M on $2.0B of revenue reflect a fabless model with real pricing power.
Cash of $800.9M against $134.0M of debt is a large net cash position, much of which has funded steady buybacks.
The expansion into power conversion and other mixed-signal content adds chips per device, which is how a supplier grows in a flat unit market.
Holding the audio socket across many product generations demonstrates how difficult the position is to displace.
watch: Content per device, meaning the number and value of Cirrus chips in each handset. Unit volumes are flat; the only growth available is selling more into each device, and that is the figure to follow.
view: There is no polite way around the central fact about Cirrus Logic: it is largely a supplier to one customer, and that customer designs its own silicon whenever it decides a component matters enough. Everything else about the business — the margins, the cash generation, the modest multiple — is a consequence of that single structural reality, and any analysis that treats it as a diversified chip designer is wrong.

Within that constraint the position is stronger than it sounds. Audio chips are co-designed with the device over several years, tuned to its specific acoustics, and surrounded by custom software. That is not a part you swap; it is a subsystem. Cirrus has held the socket across many generations of the same customer’s products, which tells you the relationship is engineering rather than procurement. The expansion into power conversion and haptics is the right strategic response: in a market where handset units are flat, the only growth available is more chips in each device.

The financial quality is genuinely good. A 20.8% net margin, $526 million of free cash flow on $2.0 billion of revenue, $801 million of cash against $134 million of debt, and steady buybacks against a flat revenue line. At 14.5 times earnings and 10.9 times free cash flow, the market is pricing in the concentration risk rather than ignoring it, which is the correct starting point.

The risk is not gradual, and this is what makes the stock difficult to hold rather than merely cheap. Design decisions are made years in advance, so a lost socket is invisible until the revenue stops. There is no deterioration to watch for — the business looks fine until it does not. Three analysts covering a $5.7 billion company means almost nobody is checking. I regard this as a well-run, cash-generative business at a fair price with a tail risk that cannot be diversified away or forecast, and I would size a position accordingly rather than on the multiple.
bull: Content per device keeps rising as power, haptics and camera chips add to the audio socket, and a net-cash fabless designer at 11 times free cash flow buys back stock.
bear: The dominant customer brings audio in-house, and because design decisions are made years ahead, the revenue disappears without warning.
